Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones
A specific texture associated with the event

Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I have to be on guard all the time
The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: For a 55-year-old female bank teller with combat trauma, 'Bicycle' as a trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other trigger items imply interpersonal/loss and sensory trauma reminders, while bicycle is a highly specific cue with no support from threat, memory, or appraisal content and no clear combat linkage. This makes it clinically implausible rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'You can never know who will harm you' is too nonspecific relative to the rest of the profile. The threat items emphasize overt vigilance and reading faces/body language, and the appraisals also center betrayal and loss of meaning. This item implies diffuse interpersonal mistrust without a corresponding interpersonal memory or trigger pattern beyond betrayal, making the negative appraisal set less coherent with the otherwise combat/loss-focused formulation.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: The profile is otherwise organized around combat-linked threat, sensory triggers, and disjointed trauma memory, but the betrayal appraisal introduces a different interpersonal trauma theme that is not supported by the other selected items. With combat trauma, betrayal can occur, but here there are no corresponding triggers, memory content, or threat/appraisal items suggesting moral injury, friendly-fire, command betrayal, or interpersonal violation. This makes the betrayal item the main clinically incoherent element relative to the rest of the profile and formulation.

vignette: Maria Hernandez's eyes still scan the crowded bank lobby with a mixture of habit and anxiety, a vestige of her years serving in combat zones. It's been decades since she left the military, but the sounds and textures of that chaotic world continue to seep into her daily life as a bank teller. The clang of the vault door closing or the rustle of a customer's nylon jacket can transport her back to the dusty, war-torn streets of her past. The specific texture that haunts her is the rough, canvas-like fabric of military gear. She remembers the feel of it beneath her fingers as she tended to wounded comrades, the smell of sweat and blood mingling with the acrid tang of smoke and explosives. When a customer's jacket or bag brushes against her, unleashing a whiff of that same texture, Maria's heart quickens, her palms grow sweaty, and her mind begins to reel. She tries to focus on the transactions in front of her, but her gaze keeps drifting toward the security monitors above the doors, searching for signs of danger. She studies the faces of those entering the bank, parsing their body language for any hint of malice. Her coworkers have grown accustomed to her intensity, attributing it to a keen sense of customer service, but Maria knows the truth: she's constantly on guard, waiting for the other shoe to drop. Conversations about loss or tragedy can also unravel her composure. When customers share stories of their own struggles, Maria feels an overwhelming urge to flee, as if the very mention of pain and suffering might summon the darkness that lurks within her. She recalls the devastating losses she witnessed during combat – friends, civilians, innocence – and how those experiences have eroded her sense of meaning. Maria's memories of that time remain disjointed, like a puzzle with missing pieces. When she attempts to recount specific events, she becomes mired in confusion, unable to articulate what happened or when. Her story feels unreal, as if it belonged to someone else, and this sense of disconnection only exacerbates her feelings of hypervigilance. She has come to believe that the world is a treacherous place, where danger lurks around every corner. As she navigates the city streets on her daily commute, Maria's senses are on high alert, primed for the slightest sign of threat. Her hyperarousal has taken a toll on her relationships; her divorce was, in part, a casualty of her inability to shake off the constant sense of unease. It wasn't until a recent explosion at a nearby construction site sent Maria into a panic, prompting her manager to suggest she take some time off, that she realized she needed help. As she sits in her therapist's office, fidgeting with the hem of her skirt – a gesture eerily reminiscent of the nervous habits she developed during combat – Maria confesses her deep-seated fear: that if she lets her guard down, even for an instant, the darkness will consume her. With tears welling up in her eyes, Maria whispers, "I just want to feel safe again. I want to be able to tell my story without it feeling like a lie." For the first time in years, she dares to hope that maybe, just maybe, she can find a way to quiet the cacophony of threats and triggers that have ruled her life for so long.
